title: China Lays Out Fourfold AI Compute Build-Out and Enflame's $25.5B Debut Caps the Domestic Chip Wave
subhead: Beijing's MIIT five-year plan targets 9,800 eflops of intelligent computing by 2030, while Enflame's blockbuster Shanghai IPO — up 179% on its first day — shows capital markets throwing their weight behind China's domestic AI chip push as the US leaves optical transceivers off its latest blacklist update.

sections.heading: China's Fourfold AI Compute Plan Sets 2030 Target
sections.body:
China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), in a five-year industry plan released this week, set a target of 9,800 eflops of intelligent computing capacity by 2030, with 3.8 trillion yuan (US$532 billion) in cumulative information infrastructure investment over 2026-2030, the South China Morning Post reports. The plan calls for the 'orderly deployment' of AI computing clusters using 10,000 graphics cards or those running 100,000 or more cards, alongside inference facilities adapted to home-grown computing chips.

The target extends a rapid build-out already under way: China's intelligent computing capacity had reached 2,185 eflops by the end of June, up 177% year on year, with 52 facilities each equipped with more than 10,000 accelerator cards, per MIIT. Reaching the 2030 goal means more than quadrupling that June level. Capacity had already risen to about 2,450 eflops by the end of July, according to the National Data Administration. The push builds on the 'East Data, West Computing' project launched in 2022.
sections.whyItMatters: This is Beijing's clearest quantified statement yet of its compute ambitions — and it comes while US export controls still cap China's access to top-tier Nvidia parts. The fourfold target signals that system-level scale and domestic-chip adaptation, not sheer advanced-node access, are now the axes of the race.

sections.heading: Enflame's 179% Debut Completes the 'Four Little Dragons' IPO Wave
sections.body:
Enflame Technology, a Tencent-backed Nvidia challenger, surged 179% in its Shanghai debut on Friday, closing at 397 yuan with a market capitalisation of 170.9 billion yuan (US$25.5 billion), according to the SCMP. It opened at 410 yuan against an issue price of 142.18 yuan and rose as much as 234% intraday. The offering raised about 6.12 billion yuan from 43.04 million shares, with the retail tranche oversubscribed 4,073 times and an allocation rate for individuals of just 0.025%.

Enflame is the last of China's 'four little dragons' in AI chips — alongside Moore Threads, Biren Technology and MetaX Integrated Circuits — to go public. Its gains stood out against a falling market: the Star 50 Index fell 1% and the CSI 300 dropped 0.8% on the day. Tencent's stake rose about 20% to nearly 35 billion yuan.
sections.whyItMatters: The staggering IPO metrics show mainland capital markets enthusiastically pricing domestic AI chip champions as strategic assets, not just commercial bets. Each successful public listing gives Beijing's self-sufficiency push more financial firepower to fund the compute build-out outlined in the MIIT plan.

sections.heading: US Leaves Optical Transceivers off the Ban List — For Now
sections.body:
The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has published its final decision updating its equipment authorisation rules, easing market anxiety over a potential ban on Chinese optical transceivers, the SCMP reports. The rule, adopted in July and finalised on Friday, tightens authorisation for devices containing components made by entities on the Covered List — a US blacklist of foreign equipment deemed a national-security risk — but did not target optical transceivers, the data-centre components central to AI networks.

The decision calmed speculation after an August Reuters report said the Trump administration was drafting measures to block new Chinese optical transceiver models from the US market this year. Shares responded: Zhongji Innolight closed up about 4% in Shenzhen and 4.37% in Hong Kong, while Eoptolink gained nearly 3%. Chinese suppliers hold a commanding position in a domain that is becoming increasingly central to AI infrastructure.
sections.whyItMatters: The optics sector is a rare case where Washington has held back from restricting Chinese suppliers despite AI-fuelled scrutiny. The reprieve is real but conditional — the Covered List mechanism remains in place, and the sector could still face action if transceiver dependency is reframed as a national-security exposure.

sections.heading: OpenAI Weighs a Slowdown as AI Safety Alarm Grows Ahead of Xi-Trump Summit
sections.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told employees in a company-wide meeting this week that the firm was considering slowing down its AI development, and may coordinate any slowdown with other leading labs, according to Bloomberg, as reported by the SCMP. The remarks come amid a flurry of cybersecurity breaches, internal whistle-blowing and declining visibility into model safety that has alarmed experts in Silicon Valley.

Paul Christiano, an AI safety researcher who recently joined OpenAI's non-profit board to serve on its safety and security committee, warned on Thursday of a 'catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term' on the current trajectory. The unease is mounting ahead of a Xi-Trump summit, with US-China tensions undercutting AI safety cooperation, the SCMP reported.
sections.whyItMatters: A coordination conversation among leading labs would mark a genuine shift from the 'move fast' posture that has defined the current AI race. But the incentive structure — first-mover advantage and the competitive pressure from Chinese model makers — makes any pause hard to sustain, and the timing compounds US anxiety ahead of the bilateral summit.

sections.heading: Ant Pushes a Global Standard for AI-Agent Payments
sections.body:
Ant International, the overseas affiliate of Ant Group, open-sourced its Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP) on GitHub on Friday, putting it forward as a potential global standard for how AI agents securely pay for goods, the SCMP reports. The protocol is built on Ant's Alipay+ cross-border network, which connects 10 major Asian digital wallets serving 1.5 billion consumer accounts in an initial phase, covering Alipay, AlipayHK, Singapore's Starryblu and South Korea's KakaoPay and Toss.

Separately, Ant International announced a joint effort with credit card giants Visa and Mastercard on a 'know-your-agent' (KYA) framework to standardise identity verification for AI agents across card networks, wallets and marketplaces globally, the company said.
sections.whyItMatters: Whoever sets the payment and identity standards for autonomous AI agents could capture the rails of machine-to-machine commerce, much as Alipay+ did for human cross-border payments. Ant's move — pairing an open protocol with credit-card alliances — is an early bid by a Chinese fintech to define that global layer rather than simply compete inside it.

sections.heading: Huawei's 7.2Tbps Optical Module Targets the AI Interconnect Bottleneck
sections.body:
Huawei showcased what it calls the industry's first 7.2-terabit-per-second near-packaged optics (NPO) product at the China International Optoelectronic Exposition (CIOE) in Shenzhen this week, pitching it as a fix for AI infrastructure bottlenecks, the SCMP reports. The module combines 36 channels at 200 gigabits per second each for aggregate 7.2Tbps bandwidth, according to Man Jiangwei, director of Huawei's advanced optoelectronics laboratory.

NPO replaces traditional copper wiring with light-based signals to move data between AI processors at higher speed and lower power. Man said Huawei has 'fully entered the product development stage', positioning the module alongside the 6.4Tbps optical engines developed for co-packaged optics by US chipmaker Broadcom.
sections.whyItMatters: As AI clusters scale to thousands of interlinked processors, interconnect bandwidth — not just compute silicon — is becoming a limiting factor and a new competitive front. Huawei's push, alongside the US leaving Chinese transceivers off the blacklist, keeps the optical supply chain a contested area where Chinese firms hold real technical position.

bottomLine: Friday's stories were dominated by China's two-track AI build-out: an explicit state target to quadruple intelligent computing capacity by 2030, financed by a $532 billion infrastructure plan, and capital markets pouring money into domestic chip champions — Enflame's 179% debut closing out the 'four little dragons' IPO wave. Washington, meanwhile, chose restraint in the optical transceiver sector even as it keeps the Covered List mechanism ready, and OpenAI signaled it is at least debating a slowdown in an AI race that shows no sign of easing on the Chinese side. The pattern is not a story about who 'controls' everything — it is concrete: Beijing is scaling compute at the systems level with domestic silicon, US export policy is picking its battles selectively, and the agentic-commerce and interconnect standards wars are just beginning.
sources: South China Morning Post (SCMP), Bloomberg (as reported by SCMP)
